content: Medical thermometers, traditionally mercury-in-glass devices, are used to measure human body temperature. The thermometer's tip is inserted into the mouth (oral temperature), under the armpit (axillary temperature), or into the rectum via the anus (rectal temperature). Classification by Technology The traditional mercury-filled medical thermometer operates similarly to a meteorological maximum thermometer. When the temperature rises, the mercury expands and moves up the tube. The temperature is read from the scale inscribed on the side of the thermometer. A constriction near the bulb prevents the mercury from returning to the bulb when the temperature falls, leaving the mercury column stationary in the tube. To reset the thermometer, it must be sharply swung to force the mercury back into the bulb. In the 1990s, mercury thermometers were deemed too hazardous to handle and have largely been replaced by electronic thermometers or, less commonly, thermometers using non-mercury liquids. In some regions, selling mercury-containing products, including thermometers, is illegal. Both mercury and electronic thermometers can be used orally, axillarily, or rectally. Classification by Location Oral Oral temperature measurement is only suitable for patients who can securely hold the thermometer in their mouth. This method is generally not recommended for small children or individuals who are coughing, weak, or vomiting. While fast-reacting digital thermometers have mitigated this issue, traditional mercury thermometers, which take several minutes to register a temperature, posed significant challenges. Additionally, if the patient has consumed hot or cold liquids beforehand, the reading may be inaccurate, necessitating a waiting period or an alternative method. Rectal Rectal temperature measurement, particularly when performed by someone other than the patient, should be facilitated with a lubricant, such as a water-based personal lubricant (petroleum jelly is now discouraged). Although rectal temperature is the most accurate method, it may be considered embarrassing in certain cultures or for older patients. If not performed correctly, it can cause discomfort or even pain. Rectal temperature measurement is the preferred method for infants in the general public, but from a nursing perspective, it is the least desirable route for infants. Ear and Forehead Other types of medical thermometers include tympanic thermometers, which measure the temperature of the tympanic membrane using infrared technology, and band thermometers, which are applied to the patient’s forehead.
